title: Stacking & Nesting
strapline: Up it goes, down it comes; big one, little one, all tucked inside — the toddler research of size and balance.
intent: Feed the deep toddler drive to build up and knock down, then build again — the whole cycle is the play.
Develop the fine control of placing one thing carefully on another, and the strength to lift and carry the heavy pieces.
Grow the earliest maths of size and order — the big cup won't fit inside the little one, but the little one hides inside the big.
Support persistence and problem-solving — the tower that topples is an invitation to try a steadier way.
Surface early size and quantity words — big, little, more, all gone, on top — spoken as toddlers work.
implementation: Offer graduated open-ended sets: nesting cups and bowls, wooden or cardboard blocks, stacking rings, small boxes and tins with lids, empty pots.
Sit alongside and resist rescuing the wobble — the toppling is data, and the rebuild is where the learning lives.
Narrate the size and position words as they happen ('the little cup is on top now', 'that one's too big to fit inside').
Notice each toddler's angle — the pure knocker-down, the careful stacker, the one who only wants to nest — and offer more of what grips them.
Keep pieces safe and generously sized, check tins for sharp rims, and let tidy-up become a nesting game in itself.
key_questions: How high can the tower go before it wobbles?
Which cup fits inside the big one — try it and see.
Your tower fell down — what will you do now?
Is that the biggest or the littlest one?
Where does the lid go — does it fit this tin or that one?

impact.text: Toddlers stack, build and knock down, then build again — the same experiment run on purpose, over and over.
Children nest cups and match lids to tins, working out by trying which size fits inside which.
Toddlers lift, carry and place the pieces deliberately, hands growing steadier with every careful stack.
Early size and quantity words surface at the tower — 'big one', 'more', 'on top', 'all fall down'.
When the tower topples, a toddler shrugs off help — 'me do it!' — and builds it steadier the next time.

enhancements: Nesting Russian-doll style boxes so hiding-inside becomes the surprise.
A mix of weights — light cardboard and heavier wooden blocks — so balance really matters.
Stacking rings on a post alongside loose rings with no post, for on-and-off freedom.
Tins in graduated sizes with matching lids, turning lid-matching into the puzzle.
A low mirror behind the tower so the building doubles and toppling is twice as thrilling.

playing_exploring: Toddlers combine cups, blocks and boxes their own way, with no set outcome.
Materials are tested with hands and whole-body effort — lifting, balancing, toppling.
active_learning: Children repeat the build-and-knock cycle dozens of times, refining the balance with each go.
A toppled tower is met with another attempt, not a call for rescue.
creating_thinking: Toddlers invent their own problems — can the little cup wear the big cup as a hat, will this one balance on that?
They change approach when a stack fails — a wider base, the bigger block first.
